certainty_reasoning: The romantic characterization - Wilde in love with Gray, Gray his 'officially beloved' - rests on two independent secondary sources: McKenna (Secret Life, 2008 edn, PDF pp. 194, 239) and McCormack (John Gray, 1991, pp. 50, 84, 88), with Raffalovich's first-hand account (Uranisme et Unisexualite, 1896, pp. 247-248) as near-contemporary colour; no primary attestation from either man has been read. The sexual element remains McKenna's assertion alone - McCormack explicitly leaves it open ('It is impossible to know whether Gray was Wilde's lover') - and the c. 1889 start rests on secondary tradition, so those two elements stay in the disputed block.
date_label: Documented span Feb. 1892 (Wilde publicly calls the acquaintance 'extremely recent') through 1893 (Silverpoints published; The Blackmailers June 1893); the editors note Wilde and Gray later 'fell out' (undated). The conventional c. 1889 start rests on secondary tradition.
summary: Gray was publicly tied to Wilde by February 1892, when the Daily Telegraph called him Wilde's 'protege' - a label Wilde corrected in print while praising Gray's 'perfected mode of expression'. In June 1892 Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), and after The Picture of Dorian Gray appeared, Gray 'referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so', though the editors find no evidence he was the character's original. The two fell out - the editors record the belief that Raffalovich broke the friendship up - but in De Profundis Wilde still ranked the friendship among those where 'my real life, my higher life' had been. Two independent biographers affirm the romantic bond - McKenna (Secret Life, 2008) and McCormack (John Gray, 1991), who calls the relationship 'absurdly romantic, intense, and idealized', records Gray's inscription 'To my loved master', and judges that being named Wilde's 'protege' in 1892 was 'the equivalent of being named Wilde's lover' - with Raffalovich's first-hand account (1896) as period colour. No first-person attestation from either man has been read, and McCormack leaves the sexual question open.

disputed.claim: That the bond was sexual as well as romantic, and that it ran from c. 1889 (the conventionally dated first meeting) through 1893.
disputed.asserted_by: McKenna asserts the sexual element outright - 'Sex between them did take place', Gray 'still Oscar's officially beloved' (Secret Life, 2008 edn, PDF pp. 192, 239). The c. 1889 start rests on secondary tradition; McCormack's first definitive report of the two together is summer 1889, a date she says 'fits' the unverified story of a meeting that year.
disputed.disputed_by: McCormack: 'It is impossible to know whether Gray was Wilde's lover' (John Gray, 1991, p. 88); Wilde's printed statement (Daily Telegraph, 20 Feb. 1892) that the acquaintance was 'extremely recent'; Holland & Hart-Davis note there is 'no evidence for the persistent suggestion' that Gray was the original of Dorian Gray.
disputed.grounds: No first-person sexual attestation appears in the primary material read; the verified record documents patronage, the Dorian self-identification, Gray's 'To my loved master' inscription, retrospective affection in De Profundis, and a falling-out.

sources.quote: Your writer describes the author of the brilliant fantastic lecture on 'The Modern Actor' as 'a protégé' of mine. Allow me to state that my acquaintance with Mr John Gray is, I regret to say, extremely recent, and that I sought it because he had already a perfected mode of expression both in prose and verse. … These qualities Mr John Gray possesses in a marked degree. He needs no other protection, nor, indeed, would he accept it.
sources.context: Wilde to the Editor of the Daily Telegraph, 19 February [1892], published 20 February headed puppets and actors; 'a protégé' italicised in original
sources.supports: The public 'protege' characterization and Wilde's printed denial of it ('extremely recent'), Feb. 1892
sources.provenance: PDF p. 540. Elision drops four sentences on artists needing protection; full text in long-form notes.

sources.quote: Dear Sir, Silverpoints (poems) by John Gray. We agree to issue the above book in the autumn on your undertaking the cost of the designs – block for same – paper, printing and binding of an edition not exceeding 250 copies.
sources.context: Mathews and Lane (The Bodley Head) to Wilde, 17 June 1892, Vigo Street - the publishers' agreement printed in Complete Letters; Silverpoints italicised in original.
sources.supports: Wilde personally undertook the production costs of Gray's Silverpoints - the patronage in a primary document
sources.speaker: Elkin Mathews and John Lane (The Bodley Head)

sources.quote: His book of poems, Silverpoints (Mathews and Lane, 1893), was designed by Ricketts, and initially underwritten by Wilde … before they fell out. … While there is no evidence for the persistent suggestion that he was the original of Dorian Gray, after the publication of the story he referred to himself as Dorian and allowed others in the Wilde circle to do so.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote on John Gray
sources.supports: The falling-out; the 'Dorian' self-identification with the editors' no-evidence caveat
sources.provenance: PDF p. 540. Elisions drop a cross-reference ('see p. 527') and bridge two non-adjacent footnote sentences.

sources.quote: When I compare my friendship with you to my friendship with such still younger men as John Gray and Pierre Louÿs I feel ashamed. My real life, my higher life was with them and such as they.
sources.context: Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas ('De Profundis'), HM Prison, Reading, January-March 1897
sources.supports: Wilde's retrospective valuation of the Gray friendship - 'my real life, my higher life'

sources.quote: In fact, the John Gray that Oscar met and fell in love with was a construction, an exquisite fiction, a carefully crafted sonnet of a young man, hewn and marvellously fashioned from very rough clay.
sources.context: McKenna opening his account of Gray's origins - born in Bethnal Green, son of a Woolwich Dockyard wheelwright, set to work at thirteen as an apprentice metal-turner. At PDF p. 239 McKenna adds that Gray was 'still Oscar's officially beloved'. Both are assertions, unlike the page at PDF 216, where he only poses the question whether Wilde led Gray or Gray led Wilde.
sources.supports: The romantic characterization ('fell in love with') - verified in the repo copy at the text layer
sources.provenance: PDF p. 194 (2008 edition; no printed folios).

sources.quote: John Gray was, of course, still Oscar's officially beloved, but for a while, at least, Johnson played the role of Oscar's 'new boy'.
sources.context: McKenna on Gray's standing in Wilde's affections relative to Lionel Johnson, whom he says Oscar probably became lovers with in 1890 - a second, independent McKenna passage making the sexual characterization.
sources.supports: Corroborates the romantic characterization ('officially beloved') from a second McKenna passage.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 239 (2008 edition; no printed folios).

sources.quote: Whereas Reade identified that 'dedicated homosexual' as Raffalovich, it is clear that Gray's first such attachment was actually Oscar Wilde.
sources.context: McCormack correcting Brian Reade's claim that Gray was drawn into a homosexual relationship by a 'dedicated homosexual' (Reade named Raffalovich). She elsewhere leaves the sexual question open - 'It is impossible to know whether Gray was Wilde's lover' (p. 88) - so this is a statement of Gray's first homosexual attachment, not of consummation.
sources.supports: Gray's first homosexual attachment was Wilde - an independent biography's direct statement
sources.provenance: Printed p. 50 (PDF p. 67); read from the rendered page image.

sources.quote: In short, to be named in the spring of 1892 as Wilde's 'protégé' or as the original of 'Dorian Gray' was the equivalent of being named Wilde's lover.
sources.context: McCormack on the aftermath of The Star's 'Dorian' remark (6 February 1892) and the Daily Telegraph's 'literary and dramatic godfather' squib - what being publicly linked to Wilde meant in 1892.
sources.supports: The public valence of the association: named as Wilde's protege or as 'Dorian' read as lover-status
sources.provenance: Printed p. 84 (PDF p. 101); read from the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Still, the relationship was not one of cool and calculated exploitation, but in character with 'Dorian Gray' was in many ways 'absurdly romantic,' intense, and idealized. And so, despite Wilde's own infatuation with Douglas, Gray remained deeply attached to Wilde during the course of 1892.
sources.context: McCormack's assessment, immediately after her caveat that 'It is impossible to know whether Gray was Wilde's lover; that issue is of less importance than Gray's drive to efface himself...'
sources.supports: The romantic characterization - intense, idealized, mutually attached through 1892 - from a second, independent biography
sources.provenance: Printed p. 88 (PDF p. 105); read from the rendered page image.

sources.quote: It says much about the nature of Gray's feelings that, in October 1892, when his translation of Bourget's A Saint and Others appeared, Gray inscribed his copy to Wilde: 'To my loved master my dear friend Homage.'
sources.context: McCormack on Gray's presentation copy of his Bourget translation; the inscription is Gray's own hand. In the same passage Wilde is 'the poet' who that summer offered to underwrite Silverpoints.
sources.supports: Gray's own inscription - 'To my loved master' - the closest surviving first-person expression of the relationship
sources.provenance: Printed p. 88 (PDF p. 105); read from the rendered page image.

sources.quote: On permettait à ses fils de l'aduler et d'en être adulé, de se laisser appeler le nouveau boy d'Oscar.
sources.translation: His young men were allowed to flatter him and to be flattered by him in return, to let themselves be called Oscar's new boy.
sources.context: Raffalovich, writing of Wilde at the height of his fame (the passage continues with the first night of Lady Windermere's Fan). This is the passage behind McKenna's 'new boy' citation (McKenna, PDF p. 239); the sentence, including 'a ses fils', is confirmed on the rendered page image.
sources.supports: A near-contemporary's account of Wilde's young men being openly called 'Oscar's new boy' - the circle's code
sources.provenance: Printed p. 247 (PDF p. 253); read from the rendered page image.

sources.quote: Même sans mener une vie exempte de soupçons, même en prêchant la corruption, même entouré des jeunes hommes les plus voyants, les plus chatoyants de Londres, il aurait pu ne pas dégringoler.
sources.translation: Even without leading a life free of suspicion, even preaching corruption, even surrounded by the most conspicuous, most glittering young men of London, he might not have fallen.
sources.context: Raffalovich on Wilde at the height of his success, before the Douglas affair - the source of McKenna's 'preaching corruption' citation (McKenna, PDF p. 216).
sources.supports: Near-contemporary confirmation that Wilde 'preached corruption' among his young men - McKenna's cited source, now read directly
sources.provenance: Printed p. 248 (PDF p. 254); read from the rendered page image.
